name: Erik Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. What does a usual shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 58, a junior lineworker. I check the harness tags and insulated gloves at the depot, then ride out with a crew lead and carry the gear while I learn the line checks. I used to do building maintenance, so the height work is still new to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is hardest to leave at the depot?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that a careful crew can restore power without leaving a loose connection for the next shift. My partner Maren and I rent a small flat; our adult children are 25 and 32 and live independently, while we still watch every bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a short checklist can help me find the right connector, but I still read its rating before it goes near a line. Saving a few minutes at the depot doesn't change the careful part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect a small change to remove my field work because most of my day is physical. I'm still worried about money; our savings are less than a month's expenses and my pay is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking scheduled shifts and practise checking harness tags with the crew lead. I would try a new checklist only after an experienced worker showed me that it matched the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly secure about the task, but anxious about rent and the bills we already have. A small office change doesn't give me enough savings to stop worrying about a slow week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What item would you double-check before the crew left the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read the harness inspection tag and compare it with the date on the equipment sheet. If they disagreed, I'd ask the lead to hold the gear until we knew which record was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you trust a new checklist without asking the lead to read it with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the crew had used it on several jobs and found that the connector numbers matched the parts. I would still inspect each item myself because that is part of what keeps the job safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster dispatch is useful if the crew still gets enough time to check the site. A schedule cannot show the lead whether the access gate is locked or the shoulder is soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry the company could put higher callout targets on a junior crew if dispatch gets faster. That might cut training time or leave me with fewer paid hours, and I have few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the lineworkers' association and ask what happens to junior hours when dispatch changes. I would keep working field shifts and learn the new AI dispatch tool only after the lead showed how to report a bad route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about hours, but I can learn a tool once someone has shown that it works. I'm not young enough to spend a year experimenting without knowing whether the pay will continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show you that the company had changed the work rather than just the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the lead gives the crew less time for each callout or my training shifts disappear, I'd ask for the old and new schedules side by side. Then I'd know whether the tool changed the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the association to ask management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want an explanation of the new callout target and how much paid practice a junior worker gets. I don't expect an unchanged roster, but I want the company to say how it will handle the transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the utility should tell field workers how many paid shifts it expects to keep before people plan their rent around them. AGI can do the dispatch thinking, but robots come later and the crew still has physical work for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years until robots is not the same as three years of wages. I could lose hours before 2031, and at 58 I don't have enough savings to wait for a distant vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd join the association and ask the utility to give junior crews paid training before cuts. In 2028 I would not transfer to records or planning as a safe career, because AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if the utility offers its paid pole-connector course, I'd enroll and keep earning on field shifts while available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because my pay and my partner's part-time wages cover our rent. A paid course gives me something to work toward, but I cannot assume a new certificate guarantees work until retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner change first if your shift hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that our adult children have their own expenses, so I won't assume they can pay our rent. We would check my recent pay stubs together and find out whether overtime shifts are available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the pole-connector course useful to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs hands-on practice and a paid place in the work schedule. I would ask another lineworker to show me the task, and I would check whether the credential appears on my training record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should use five years to give crews proper practice and publish the hours it expects to offer. The robot date is 2034, so the field-work window is longer than in the last picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when AGI arrives and 66 when robots arrive. I would have time to improve at linework, but I might still need wages at 66 because my savings are very low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the lead to sign off each practical qualification and ask the employer whether any retirement contributions have been made for me. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd keep taking paid shifts and complete the utility's connector course if funded. I'd compare any written account statement with monthly bills before choosing a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but five years gives me time to check my options before the thinking work changes. I won't assume a pension amount or a job opening until I see the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the employer to plan a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a statement showing what contributions, if any, are in my name, plus the paid shifts the employer expects to schedule. I don't want to mistake an estimate for money I can actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think of taking a desk role until the robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't count on dispatch or records as a bridge, because AGI can do that thinking work by 2031. I'd compare real field shifts and any written retirement statement instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the utility to show the crew plan and for me to get my own retirement figures in writing. I wouldn't tell another worker that more notice means their job or pension is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 when AGI arrives and 71 when the robots do. I may still need income before that robot date, but I don't know whether the utility will keep me on the roster or what my retirement account will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask for any current retirement-contribution statement and keep each linework qualification documented. In 2037, if I'm still working, I'd check the actual roster and verified account figures with my partner before deciding whether to continue or retire; I wouldn't use a desk plan as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ten-year warning helps, but my savings still cover less than a month today. I'm anxious about present bills and uncertain income at an age when I had hoped to be winding down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner before making that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what our monthly expenses would be if my wages stop and what income we can actually count on. I wouldn't call a possible pension a plan until we've seen written figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work would you be willing to do in 2037 if the utility still has shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue field work if the company offers paid hours and the lead says I'm qualified for the task. At 69, I would not assume another employer will take me or that a course creates a vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose paid work before I know how much retirement income I have. A written account statement, a paid course, and enough notice to understand the roster would help me plan with my partner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want a written estimate of my own retirement income, not a guess. If the utility changes hours, I need to know the actual number before my partner and I decide whether I can stop working.

headlineQuote: I want a written estimate of my own retirement income, not a guess.
portrait: Erik is a **58-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner and two grown children.
He values **hands-on instruction** and uses new tools after experienced workers check them.
His **thin savings** and lower pay make retirement uncertain rather than assured.
He wants paid practical training and **verified contribution figures** before choosing whether to keep working.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him because a crew change could precede his access to clear retirement figures.
whatWouldHelp: A written **account statement**, paid training and notice of roster changes would help him plan with his partner.
